title: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the right, ordered top to bottom. This is the last node of each level in a level order traversal.
shortTitle: Right View of a Binary Tree (Last Node of Each Level)

s1_definition.profdef: Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the last node dequeued (when the index equals `levelSize - 1`). Those last nodes, top to bottom, are the right-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).
s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the right edge, you see only the rightmost approver on each rank, because they block the view of everyone to their left on that rank. Collecting the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom is the right view.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the last node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the last node dequeued (when the index equals `levelSize - 1`). Those last nodes, top to bottom, are the right-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the right edge, you see only the rightmost approver on each rank, because they block the view of everyone to their left on that rank. Collecting the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom is the right view.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; capture the last node of each level into the result.

sections.s2_technical:
The traversal is standard BFS with the level-size snapshot. Inside the drain loop, compare the loop index to `levelSize - 1`; when they match, that node is the last of its level, so add its value to the result. Enqueue children left then right as usual. The result ends up as the rightmost node per level in top-to-bottom order.

For example a tree with levels [1], [2,3], [4] yields right view [1,3,4], where level 3 has only the single node 4 even though it descends from the left side. That example shows the right view is not simply the right spine; it is the last node per level regardless of which parent it came from.

A senior-level nuance is exactly that subtlety: naive candidates follow only right children and get the wrong answer when the right subtree is shorter than the left. The level-based last-node rule is correct precisely because it is defined per level, not per branch. The symmetric left view just captures the first node of each level instead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India displays a right-edge summary of its approval tree, showing the final approver on each rank, which represents the most senior approver reachable at that depth on the right flank. The display must show the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom, correctly even when the left side runs deeper. This is exactly the right view: BFS capturing the last node of each level.

The code contains a `ViewNode`, a `RightViewService` with `rightView(root)`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: root 1; level 2 is 2,3; level 3 is only 4 (left child of 2).

Step 1: Level 1 has one node. Index 0 equals levelSize-1 (0), so record 1. Enqueue 2,3.

Step 2: Level 2 drains 2 then 3. Index 0 (node 2) is not last; index 1 (node 3) equals levelSize-1 (1), so record 3. Enqueue 4 (child of 2).

Step 3: Level 3 has only node 4. Index 0 equals levelSize-1 (0), so record 4. Even though 4 descends from the left side, it is the last node of its level.

Step 4: Right view is [1,3,4].

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Right view: [1, 3, 4]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tree rooted at 1 (level 3 only node 4, from left)
    │
    ▼
  RightViewService.rightView()  (last node per level)
    │ L1 last=1 → [1]
    │ L2 last=3 → [1,3]
    │ L3 last=4 → [1,3,4]   (4 from left side, still last of its level)
    ▼
  Output: [1, 3, 4]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The right view of a binary tree is the set of nodes visible when standing on its right side, and the correct definition is the last node of each level, top to bottom. I compute it with Tree BFS and the level-size snapshot, and inside the drain loop I compare the loop index to the level size minus one; when they match, that node is the last of its level, so I add its value to the result. Children are enqueued left then right as usual.

The subtlety that I always highlight is that the right view is not simply the chain of right children. If the left subtree runs deeper than the right, the last node on a lower level can descend entirely from the left side, and a naive right-spine walk would miss it. Defining the answer per level rather than per branch is exactly what makes the level-based last-node rule correct, and the symmetric left view is the same algorithm capturing the first node of each level.

In my work at the National Bank of India this produced a right-edge approval summary showing the final approver on each rank, representing the most senior approver reachable at that depth on the right flank, and it had to stay correct even when the left side of the hierarchy ran deeper. Capturing the last node of each level with BFS gave that summary accurately, and being able to explain why it is not the right spine is what demonstrates genuine command of the problem.
